references.text: The psalmist speaks of how no one can buy their way out of death with wealth—a parallel to the idea that it profits a person nothing to gain the whole world but lose themselves.
Ecclesiastes declares that all is vanity and emptiness, emphasizing that worldly gain has no value for the soul.

Ecclesiastes describes how humans leave the world just as naked as they came, unable to take with them anything they have worked for—paralleling the truth that it profits nothing to gain the whole world.
Satan says that a person will give all they have for their life—this highlights the value of life compared to material things.
Matthew's parallel passage where Jesus asks what it profits a person if they gain the whole world but lose their soul, and what a person can give in exchange for their soul.
Mark's parallel passage with the same statement from Jesus that it does not profit a person to gain the whole world and lose their soul.

Paul counts everything he once regarded as gain as loss for the sake of Christ, and considers all things as rubbish so that he may win Christ—a thematic parallel to giving up the world for the salvation of the soul.
John warns against loving the world or anything in it, for the world and its desires are passing away—underscoring the futility of gaining the world at the expense of the soul.
James reminds us of life's transience—life is like a vapor that appears for a little while and then vanishes—emphasizing that worldly gain is fleeting.
